Our foundation is here to help.

approach.mission_intro_html: The Foundation runs programs for teachers and coordinators, and equip them with mentors and funding.Yes, monthly stipend
mission: More than half of every program is practice. Each starts with an intensive and moves quickly into practical work: teachers lead lessons with children, while coordinators bring real situations from their schools and work through them together. A mentor stays with the group throughout.
We use approaches we trust and that have been well studied, such as inquiry-based learning, activity-based learning, and project work. We don’t have a new pedagogy to sell.
The test is simple: does it still work in a regular class of 35 on a Tuesday morning?

fellowship.title_html: dear teachers,
intro: You see the effects of years of classroom disruption better than anyone. We want to give you time to learn, try things out, and work through what happens in the classroom with a mentor.
We start with the later years of primary school and the beginning of middle school — when many children begin to lose interest in learning.

benefits.title: Specific teaching practices
benefits.body: Intensives where we explore and try specific teaching practices.
questions: “how do you get a class’s attention without raising your voice?”
“how do you build motivation that doesn’t depend on grades?”
“how do you start a lesson with a real question?”
“how do you get children to look for answers themselves instead of trying to guess what the teacher wants to hear?”

benefits.title: Practice with children
benefits.body: After the intensive, participants spend several weeks teaching children and go over their lessons with a mentor every week. The point is to bring what they learn back to their own classrooms.

benefits.title: A stipend for your time
benefits.body:
You have more than enough work without us, so we pay participants a stipend for both the training and the practice with children.
If we believe a teacher’s time matters, it makes sense to act like it.

leaders.title_html: dear coordinators,
intro: Strong teachers need schools where they can do good work and want to stay. That’s why we work not only with teachers, but also with people who shape the teams around them.
Our first program for coordinators is being developed together with rakazim themselves. The first pilot is under way with a closed cohort.

benefits.title: Leading without formal authority
benefits.body:
Rakazim are teachers too. They teach their own classes and help a whole team work better, often without formal authority over the people they lead.
How do you move a team forward when the people in it don’t report to you?

benefits.title: Feedback that actually helps
benefits.body:
How do you give feedback that people can use, support colleagues, and help them grow?
Participants bring real situations from their schools and work through them together with a mentor.

benefits.title: Making room for the work that matters
benefits.body:
How do you distribute the workload across the team and make time for everyone to grow?
The program also covers the practical systems and projects that keep a department running without letting coordination take over the time meant for teaching.

results: Our first intensive in Tbilisi focused on inquiry-based education. We surveyed the teachers after the intensive and again after several weeks of teaching children with weekly mentoring.

The understanding scale starts at “I understand, with questions” and ends at “I can use it”. On the fundamentals, what an inquiry lesson is for, how it differs from a merely engaging one and what the teacher does, four in five answers are now at “I can use it”, up from two in five. On the craft, such as moderating without hinting and helping children through uncertainty, the share went from 15% to 27%, and every teacher now has at least one aspect there; after the intensive, half of them had none.
tbilisi.quote: “Much less likely to lead children toward the right answer, and more attentive to how they reason.”
tbilisi.quote_note: One of the teachers · that’s the change we’re looking for
results_after: Ten of twelve will use these techniques in their own classrooms. Group dynamics is the one thing practice did not make easier, so we’re adding more practice and mentoring around it. Three-quarters of the children surveyed said they would like lessons like these at school.
tbilisi.caveat: Encouraging results, but from a small, unusually friendly setting, compared cohort to cohort. We’ll see how they hold up in regular classrooms.

note.title: The team
note.body: We bring together teacher-development specialists and practicing teachers. We’re also building a circle of experienced Israeli educators and researchers who can challenge our assumptions and help us understand the school system from the inside.

questions.a: We currently focus on practicing teachers in the later years of primary school and the beginning of middle school. If you work with another age group, you can still get in touch and tell us about your experience.
We teach teachers to use AI — and to teach children how to use it — instead of training AI to replace teachers.

We interleave theory and workshops with practice on real cases: organized practice with kids for teachers, real school cases for coordinators. And live sessions with mentors in small groups every week.
Yes. We pay participants for the training and the subsequent practice with children. The amount and payment arrangements will be provided with the details of each program.

questions.q: Can a school or municipality work with Morim?
questions.a: Yes. We’re interested in working with schools, networks, and municipalities that want to bring our programs to their teachers or coordinators. We’re also looking for experienced educators who can help us build the programs.
